topics.observableQuestion: When can allele frequencies be counted directly, and when are they inferred through a model?
topics.learningGoal: Calculate allele and genotype frequencies with correct denominators and distinguish observations from equilibrium expectations.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: Diploid genotypes contribute two allele copies per individual. A frequency is a part divided by its corresponding whole. Squaring and square roots link different quantities only under the stated model.

retrieval.prompt: From 36 AA, 48 Aa and 16 aa, calculate p.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: A copies = 2(36) + 48 = 120; all copies = 200, so p = 0.60.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Solve one supplied population case and state whether its allele frequency was counted or inferred, including a relevant assumption.
criteria: Show the denominator or q² step.
Label observed versus expected and state a model limit.

localWalkthrough.status: complete-ordered-narration; illustrations and equivalence review pending

frames.title: Populations and allele counts
frames.scenario: A diploid population sample contains 36 AA, 48 Aa and 16 aa individuals. Calculate A and a allele counts and frequencies directly from the observations.
orderedExplanation: Count 100 individuals and therefore 200 allele copies at this autosomal locus.
Count A copies: 2(36) + 48 = 120; count a copies: 2(16) + 48 = 80.
Divide each count by 200 to obtain p = 0.60 and q = 0.40.
frames.conclusion: The observed allele frequencies are 0.60 and 0.40. Direct counting does not require assuming Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Allele and genotype frequencies
frames.scenario: Using p = 0.60 and q = 0.40, calculate Hardy–Weinberg expected genotype frequencies and compare them with the observed 36/48/16 sample.
orderedExplanation: Calculate p² = 0.36, 2pq = 0.48 and q² = 0.16.
Check that the three expected frequencies sum to 1.
Compare with observed genotype frequencies 36/100, 48/100 and 16/100 while keeping observed and expected labels separate.
frames.conclusion: The observed frequencies match these expectations in this sample. That numerical match alone does not prove that every equilibrium condition holds or that the frequencies will remain constant across generations.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Equilibrium assumptions
frames.scenario: A large population mates randomly at one locus but receives immigrants carrying a different allele frequency. Which part of the Hardy–Weinberg model is challenged?
orderedExplanation: Identify gene flow as movement of alleles into the population.
Recognize that random mating does not cancel a change in allele frequencies caused by immigration.
Separate conditions affecting genotype arrangement from conditions maintaining allele frequencies across generations.
frames.conclusion: The no-migration condition is violated. The population could form genotype proportions near p²:2pq:q² after random mating while its p and q have changed through gene flow.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Solving and checking
frames.scenario: In a fictional fully penetrant recessive-trait model, 9% of a population shows the recessive phenotype. Assuming Hardy–Weinberg conditions, estimate q, p and the carrier frequency.
orderedExplanation: Set q² = 0.09 only under the stated recessive-phenotype and equilibrium assumptions.
Take q = 0.30 and calculate p = 1 − q = 0.70.
frames.conclusion: The estimated allele frequencies are q = 0.30 and p = 0.70; the expected carrier frequency is 0.42. These are model-based estimates, not directly counted genotypes.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: A model and its limits
frames.scenario: A sample contains 45 AA, 45 Aa and 10 aa individuals. Calculate p directly and compare the observed genotype frequencies with Hardy–Weinberg expectations.
orderedExplanation: Count A copies: 90 + 45 = 135 out of 200, so p = 0.675 and q = 0.325.
Calculate expectations p² = 0.455625, 2pq = 0.43875 and q² = 0.105625.
Compare with observed frequencies 0.45, 0.45 and 0.10 without demanding exact equality in a finite sample.
frames.conclusion: The direct allele count gives p = 0.675. The small observed–expected differences require an appropriate sampling and model assessment before supporting a claim of a particular evolutionary cause.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does direct allele counting from observed diploid genotypes require equilibrium?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. It uses the observed copies; equilibrium is needed for particular predictions or inference shortcuts.

topics.observableQuestion: How can the same frequency change arise through different mechanisms?
topics.learningGoal: Separate mutation, selection, drift, movement and mating effects, using supplied population data to compare explanations.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: Allele frequencies track copies across a defined population. Genotype proportions can change without changing allele totals. A trend alone does not establish its cause.

retrieval.prompt: Do the sampled p values 0.60, 0.675 and 0.65 show a steady rise?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: No. They rise and then decline; the mechanism also remains unresolved from those counts alone.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Revise a selection or resistance claim with a measured frequency change, a mechanism and one alternative needing evidence.

localWalkthrough.status: complete-ordered-narration; illustrations and equivalence review pending

frames.title: Mutation and selection
frames.scenario: A fictional bacterial population contains a rare resistance variant before an antibiotic exposure. Its frequency later rises. Separate variant origin from the change in representation.
orderedExplanation: Identify mutation or prior inheritance as the source of the existing variant.
During exposure, compare survival and reproduction of carriers and non-carriers.
Explain the later frequency change through differential contribution to descendants rather than need-directed mutation.
frames.conclusion: Selection can increase a pre-existing resistance variant's representation. The exposure does not show that bacteria intentionally produced the exact mutation they needed.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Chance and population size
frames.scenario: Two simulated populations begin with p = 0.50. One samples ten reproductive contributors and the other samples one thousand. Predict which is more likely to show large random frequency swings and distinguish founder and bottleneck cases.
orderedExplanation: Recognize random sampling as the mechanism in both simulations.
A smaller sample generally shows larger proportional fluctuations.
A founder event samples colonists from a source; a bottleneck sharply reduces an existing population before later recovery.
frames.conclusion: The smaller population is more prone to large random swings in this model. Founder and bottleneck effects are different histories that can both intensify drift.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Movement and mating
frames.scenario: A receiving population has 100 diploid individuals with p = 0.60. Ten immigrants each carry AA. Calculate the new allele frequency before reproduction, then contrast a change in mating pattern alone.
orderedExplanation: The original population has 120 A copies among 200 total copies.
Add 20 A copies from ten AA immigrants, giving 140/220.
Calculate p ≈ 0.6364; a mating-pattern change without differential reproduction or other forces can instead alter genotype proportions while leaving allele counts unchanged.
frames.conclusion: Immigration changes p to about 0.6364 in this model. Non-random mating alone need not change p and q, even when it changes heterozygote frequency.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Resistance and evidence
frames.scenario: An antibiotic-exposed sample becomes enriched for a resistance allele. A comparison sample also changes, but it passed through a severe random bottleneck. What evidence could separate selection from drift?
orderedExplanation: Compare replicated exposed and unexposed groups under similar sampling conditions.
Measure whether the allele is associated with differential survival or reproduction during exposure.
Track bottlenecks and starting frequencies so random sampling remains an explicit alternative.
frames.conclusion: A repeated exposure-linked advantage would support selection more directly than a frequency change alone. A bottleneck can change frequencies by chance and must be considered.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Testing explanations
frames.scenario: The supplied population samples are 36/48/16, 45/45/10 and 42/46/12 for AA/Aa/aa. Calculate p for each and evaluate “the allele rose steadily because of selection.”
orderedExplanation: Use the two-copy denominator in each 100-individual sample.
Calculate p values 0.60, 0.675 and 0.65.
Notice the rise followed by a decline, then ask what evidence distinguishes selection from drift, migration and sampling.
frames.conclusion: The allele did not rise steadily. The observations show a changing sampled frequency, while the cause remains unresolved without further evidence.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Can non-random mating alone alter genotype proportions without changing p and q?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: Yes, under the stated model without other forces or differential reproductive contribution.

topics.observableQuestion: How do boundaries, units and time affect a population-growth answer?
topics.learningGoal: Estimate abundance and density, calculate demographic change and rates, and compare bounded growth models.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: Counts, area and elapsed time have different units. Population gains and losses must use one boundary and interval. A model equation expresses specified assumptions, not every cause.

retrieval.prompt: From N₀ = 1000, B = 120, I = 30, D = 70 and E = 20 over ten days, give final N and absolute daily change.
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Final N = 1060; absolute change rate = 60/10 = 6 individuals/day.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use a sampling or growth calculation to support a prediction, including units and one design/model limit.

localWalkthrough.status: complete-ordered-narration; illustrations and equivalence review pending

frames.title: Size and density
frames.scenario: A fictional area contains 240 individuals in 12 hectares. Calculate density and explain why the same density could occur in a population of a different total size.
orderedExplanation: Divide the count by area: 240/12 = 20.
Attach units: 20 individuals per hectare.
Construct a comparison such as 100 individuals in 5 hectares, also 20 per hectare, while retaining different population totals.
frames.conclusion: Density is 20 individuals/ha. Equal density does not imply equal total population size or identical spatial arrangement.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Sampling populations
frames.scenario: Five one-square-metre quadrats contain 2, 8, 4, 10 and 6 individuals. Estimate abundance in a comparable 200 m² habitat.
orderedExplanation: Add the counts: 30 individuals across 5 m².
Calculate mean density: 30/5 = 6 individuals/m².
Multiply by 200 m² to estimate 1200 individuals, assuming the sample represents the habitat.
frames.conclusion: The estimate is 1200 individuals. It is not a complete census; patchiness, sampling placement and detection can affect its reliability.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Four demographic processes
frames.scenario: A population starts at 1000. Over ten days it records 120 births, 30 immigrants, 70 deaths and 20 emigrants. Calculate net change and final size.
orderedExplanation: Add gains: 120 + 30 = 150.
Add losses: 70 + 20 = 90.
Subtract to obtain ΔN = 60, then add to the starting size: 1060.
frames.conclusion: The net change is +60 individuals and the final population size is 1060 under this complete-count model.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Rates and denominators
frames.scenario: Use ΔN = 60, initial N = 1000 and Δt = 10 days to calculate absolute daily change, interval per-initial-individual change and its daily average.
orderedExplanation: Calculate ΔN/Δt = 60/10 = 6 individuals/day.
Calculate ΔN/Ninitial = 60/1000 = 0.06 over the interval.
Divide the interval value by ten to obtain an average 0.006 per day per initial individual.
frames.conclusion: The three summaries are 6 individuals/day, 0.06 per initial individual over ten days, and 0.006 per day per initial individual. The last is an average based on the initial denominator, not a directly fitted continuous intrinsic rate.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Exponential and logistic models
frames.scenario: Compare two discrete models starting at N = 100 with r = 0.2 per step: exponential Nnext = N + rN and logistic Nnext = N + rN(1 − N/K), with K = 500.
orderedExplanation: Exponential next size is 100 + 0.2(100) = 120.
Compare the density-dependent factor while retaining the same initial size, step and r.
frames.conclusion: The first step gives 120 versus 116. In the logistic model, the additional factor reduces growth as N approaches the stated K.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Feedback and changing limits
frames.scenario: A fictional population initially stabilizes near 500, but a drought reduces available habitat and resources. Evaluate the claim that its carrying capacity must remain 500 forever.
orderedExplanation: Identify K as a model summary of support under particular conditions.
Link the environmental change to altered resource availability and possibly a different effective K.
Consider delayed population responses and other losses rather than forcing the old curve onto the new conditions.
frames.conclusion: The earlier value need not remain valid. A changing environment can alter the support conditions, and the population may respond with delays or fluctuations.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Are 6 individuals/day and 0.006 per day per initial individual the same numerical quantity?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. They summarize the same change with different denominators and units.

topics.observableQuestion: How do interactions and history shape a community's possible future?
topics.learningGoal: Compare life histories, interaction mechanisms, cycles and succession, then make a qualified ecological recommendation.
topics.priorKnowledgeSupport: An interaction's effect must be measured for each partner. Correlation differs from a causal mechanism. Communities carry biological and environmental legacies after disturbance.

retrieval.prompt: Why does soil remaining after disturbance matter when distinguishing primary and secondary succession?
retrieval.comparisonGuide: Retained soil and biological legacies change starting conditions and can support recovery pathways unlike development on bare rock.

evidenceSlip.prompt: Use one interaction or restoration dataset to recommend a bounded next step, with evidence and a meaningful uncertainty or tradeoff.
criteria: Connect it to a plausible mechanism or action.
Retain alternatives and relevant local perspectives.

localWalkthrough.status: complete-ordered-narration; illustrations and equivalence review pending

frames.title: Life-history strategies
frames.scenario: Compare a fictional species producing many small offspring with little parental care and another producing fewer offspring with greater investment. Use r/K language cautiously.
orderedExplanation: Describe the measured traits rather than beginning with a fixed label.
Relate offspring number, size, timing and survival under the stated conditions.
Use r- and K-associated tendencies as an idealized comparison while allowing mixed traits and environmental context.
frames.conclusion: The species show contrasting investment patterns, but real life histories occupy continua. A few traits do not place every organism into two rigid universal boxes.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Interactions and their effects
frames.scenario: Classify three fictional interactions: both partners show improved reproductive output; one benefits while the other's measured outcome is unchanged; one benefits while the other is harmed.
orderedExplanation: Use the defined measured effect for each partner.
Assign +/+ to mutualism, +/0 to commensalism and +/− to an antagonistic interaction such as parasitism or predation depending on mechanism.
Avoid choosing a precise mechanism solely from the signs.
frames.conclusion: The effect pattern helps classify the relationship, while the biological mechanism distinguishes interactions sharing the same sign pattern.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Competition and defence
frames.scenario: The supplied plant comparison gives mean A mass 4.0 in five-A pots, 3.0 in ten-A pots and 2.4 in mixed five-A/five-B pots. What comparisons address density and neighbour identity?
orderedExplanation: Compare five-A with ten-A pots for an intraspecific density contrast.
Compare ten-A with mixed pots at ten total plants to hold total density constant while changing neighbour composition.
Retain replication and resource measurements as limits on a specific causal claim.
frames.conclusion: The mixed pots have lower mean A mass than the same-total-density A-only pots. This supports a neighbour-composition effect in the dataset, while the exact resource mechanism requires more evidence.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Population cycles
frames.scenario: A fictional prey curve peaks before a predator curve. Explain a plausible interaction and an alternative cause that the graph alone cannot exclude.
orderedExplanation: Read the time axis and identify the lag between sampled peaks.
Propose that increased prey availability supports later predator reproduction or survival.
Consider shared environmental drivers, other prey and sampling effects before claiming a unique cause.
frames.conclusion: The lag is consistent with a predator–prey interaction, but correlation and timing alone do not prove that this mechanism fully explains the cycle.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Succession and disturbance
frames.scenario: Compare community development on newly exposed rock with recovery after a fire that leaves soil and some surviving organisms. Avoid predicting one inevitable final community.
orderedExplanation: Use the absence of developed soil as a key feature of the primary-succession example.
Use retained soil and biological legacies in the secondary-succession example.
Compare colonization, dispersal, conditions and later disturbance as influences on the pathways.
frames.conclusion: The two starting conditions support different recovery processes and timescales. Neither case guarantees a universal fixed climax community.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

frames.title: Ecological decisions and communication
frames.scenario: A fictional Canadian wetland project proposes restoration based on one season of higher plant abundance. What evidence would strengthen a recommendation?
orderedExplanation: Define the intended outcomes, including biodiversity, water conditions and relevant community priorities.
Compare with suitable reference or untreated sites across enough time to address seasonal variation.
Record sampling methods, possible tradeoffs and Indigenous and local perspectives through appropriate respectful engagement rather than inventing agreement.
frames.conclusion: One season's abundance result supports a limited observation, not complete restoration success. A recommendation should connect measured outcomes with uncertainties, alternatives and the perspectives needed for the decision.
frames.status: narration-bound; reviewed illustration and rendered sequencing pending

checkpoint.prompt: Does higher abundance of one plant automatically show greater biodiversity?
checkpoint.comparisonGuide: No. Abundance of one species and diversity are different outcomes that need separate measurements.
